accepted.question_text: Let M be a closed (that is, compact and boundaryless), simply connected 3-manifold. Must M be homeomorphic to the 3-sphere S^3? This is the 3-dimensional case of the broader Poincare conjecture discussed on the page, and in the source it is explicitly identified as the Millennium Problem formulation of the conjecture.

evidence.quote: Any simply connected, closed 3-manifold is the same as the 3-sphere.
The conjecture was proved in 2003 by the Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman, using ideas of Richard Hamilton from the early 1980s.

accepted.question_text: Does the complexity class P equal the complexity class NP? In other words, if a computational problem has solutions that can be verified in polynomial time, does it follow that the problem itself can also be solved in polynomial time?

evidence.quote: The problem of determining whether \({\mathbf P} = \mathbf{NP}\) is the most important open problem in theoretical computer science.
The question asks whether computational problems whose solutions can be verified quickly can also be solved quickly.

accepted.question_text: For a projective complex manifold, is every Hodge class algebraic? Equivalently, in the setting described on the page, are the relevant cohomology classes always generated by classes coming from subvarieties of the manifold?

evidence.quote: The Hodge conjecture states that certain cohomology groups studied by Hodge over certain nice complex varieties are generated by the classes of subvarieties.
Every Hodge class on a projective complex manifold is algebraic.

accepted.question_text: Consider the Riemann zeta function zeta(s), initially defined for Re s > 1 by the infinite sum zeta(s) = sum_{n=1}^infty 1/n^s and analytically continued to the complex plane except for a simple pole at s = 1. Do all of its nontrivial zeroes lie on the critical line Re s = 1/2?

evidence.quote: The Riemann hypothesis is perhaps the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics. It concerns the nontrivial zeroes of the Riemann zeta function, which is defined for \({\text{Re } s > 1 }\) by the infinite sum
The nontrivial zeroes of the zeta function lie on the line \({\text{Re }s=\frac12.}\)

accepted.question_text: Can one give a rigorous, axiomatized Yang-Mills theory that is internally logically consistent and also prove that the theory has a positive mass gap, meaning a strictly positive lower bound for the masses of the particles it predicts, equivalently the difference between the vacuum energy and the next lowest energy state is positive?

evidence.page: Yang-Mills Existence and Mass Gap middle paragraph
evidence.quote: In particular, successful applications of the theory to experiments and simplified models have involved a "mass gap," which is formally defined as the difference between the default energy in a vacuum and the next lowest energy state.

evidence.page: Yang-Mills Existence and Mass Gap middle paragraph
evidence.quote: A solution of the Millennium Problem will include both a set of formal axioms that characterize the theory and show that it is internally logically consistent, as well as a proof that there is some strictly positive lower bound on the masses of particles predicted by the theory.

accepted.question_text: Given any initial condition v_0 = v(x,0), where v is a velocity field in three dimensions, do there exist a velocity field v(x,t) and a pressure function p(x,t) satisfying the Navier-Stokes equations in R^3 or in the periodic three-dimensional torus R^3/Z^3 for all relevant times, and if the initial data v_0 is smooth, must there be a smooth solution? In the non-periodic case, the source also requires additional conditions preventing excessive growth as |x| tends to infinity.

evidence.page: Navier-Stokes Existence and Smoothness opening paragraph
evidence.quote: The Millennium Problem has two parts; there are existence and smoothness questions for solutions in \({\mathbb R}^3,\) and existence and smoothness questions for solutions in \({\frac{{\mathbb R}^3}{{\mathbb Z}^3}},\) a three-dimensional torus--this is the so-called periodic case.

Given any initial condition \( v_0 = v({\mathbf x},0)\), a vector field on \( {\mathbb R}^3, \) is there a velocity vector function \( v({\mathbf x},t) \) and a pressure function \( p({\mathbf x},t) \) that satisfy the equations? Is there a smooth solution if \( v_0\) is smooth?

accepted.question_text: Let E be an elliptic curve over the rational numbers. If the rational points on E form a finitely generated abelian group with rank n, and if L(E,s) is the associated Dirichlet-series L-function whose order of vanishing at s = 1 is called the analytic rank of E, must the rank of E equal its analytic rank? The source also notes a second, more technical part of the conjecture concerning the coefficient of (s-1)^r in the Taylor series of L(E,s) at s = 1.

evidence.quote: The integer \( n\) is called the rank of \( E,\) and half of the Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture concerns the computation of that rank.
The rank of \( E\) equals its analytic rank.
